pages.title: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB

sections.heading: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Azure HorizonDB is a fully managed database service built on PostgreSQL. It separates compute from storage: a cluster has one writer node and up to 15 reader nodes, and all of them share a single copy of the data in zone-redundant storage. Write-ahead log (WAL) processing, checkpointing, and backups run in the storage layer instead of on the compute nodes. Each cluster has a read-write endpoint that always points to the writer node, and a read-only endpoint that load-balances connections across the reader nodes. Applications connect with standard PostgreSQL drivers and tools.

This article assumes that as an architect, you've reviewed the [Azure data options](/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/technology-choices/data-options) and chose Azure HorizonDB as the solution for your workload. The guidance in this article provides architectural recommendations that are mapped to the principles of the [Well-Architected Framework pillars](/en-us/azure/well-architected/pillars).

**Technology scope**

This review focuses on the interrelated decisions for the following Azure resources:

- Azure HorizonDB

The following diagram shows where Azure HorizonDB fits in a typical application architecture.

[](_images/azure-horizon-db-architecture.svg#lightbox)

[Diagram that shows an application in its virtual network that connects through a private endpoint, over Private Link, to an Azure HorizonDB cluster that isn't deployed into the virtual network. In the single default pool, the read-write endpoint points to the writer node, and a load-balanced read-only endpoint distributes traffic across three reader nodes. The nodes span two availability zones, and the reader nodes are also high availability failover targets. All nodes share zone-resilient WAL storage and shared data storage, backed by zone-redundant Azure Storage. Microsoft Entra ID, Azure Monitor, and geo-redundant backups in a paired region are also shown. Geo-redundant backups are available only in paired regions. Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Fabric are optional.](_images/azure-horizon-db-architecture.svg#lightbox)

**Cluster, pool, and node topology**

An Azure HorizonDB cluster separates compute from storage, and organizes compute into a pool of nodes:

- **Cluster:** The top-level resource. A cluster contains a pool of compute nodes and a single shared copy of the data. Settings such as backup retention, geo-redundant backup, public access, private endpoints, and authentication apply to the whole cluster.
- **Pool:** A pool is a group of nodes that share the same compute configuration. Currently, each cluster supports a single default pool, which contains the writer node and can contain reader nodes. The pool has a read-only endpoint that load-balances connections across its reader nodes. You set the compute size, node count, high availability option, firewall rules, and parameter group for the pool, and you can stop and start it.
- **Nodes:** The writer node handles all writes through the cluster's read-write endpoint. Reader nodes serve reads through their pool's read-only endpoint. The reader nodes in the default pool are also the high availability failover targets for the writer node.
- **Storage:** All nodes in the pool share the same storage: zone-resilient WAL storage, zone-resilient shared data storage, and zone-redundant Azure Storage for backups and the WAL archive. Adding nodes doesn't copy data.

sections.heading: Reliability
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
The purpose of the Reliability pillar is to provide continued functionality by **building enough resilience and the ability to recover fast from failures**.

[Reliability design principles](/en-us/azure/well-architected/reliability/principles) provide a high-level design strategy applied for individual components, system flows, and the system as a whole.

sections.heading: Workload design checklist
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Start your design strategy based on the [design review checklist for Reliability](../reliability/checklist). Determine its relevance to your business requirements while keeping in mind the nature of your application and the criticality of its components. Extend the strategy to include more approaches as needed.

- **Identify built-in redundancy:** Storage is zone-redundant for every cluster. The WAL (Write Ahead Log), the data storage, and backups all keep copies across availability zones, so a committed transaction survives a zone failure even if the cluster has only a writer node.

    Compute isn't redundant by default. To keep the database available during a zone or node failure, or during planned maintenance, add at least one reader node. Reader nodes are readable, so the same reader nodes that protect the cluster also serve read traffic instead of sitting idle. If you rely on reader nodes for reads, size the cluster so the remaining reader nodes can still handle the read load after one of them becomes the writer node.

    Choose how compute is placed with the pool's high availability option: *ZoneRedundant* makes sure the compute nodes span at least two availability zones, *AnyZone* gives priority to provisioning success and might place all nodes in one zone, and *Disabled* runs a single node with no failover. Because reader nodes share storage, they don't need a data copy and are provisioned quickly.
- **Design the application to handle failover:** If the writer node fails, the service isolates it to prevent further writes, selects the reader node in the default pool whose applied log position is closest to the writer node, and promotes that reader node. The service waits until the promoted node is writable before pointing the read-write endpoint to it. A reader node's applied log position can lag behind the writer node's, but the WAL service makes every committed transaction durable across zones before acknowledging it. Because all nodes share storage, the promoted node has access to every committed write, so no committed transaction is lost. Open connections drop and uncommitted transactions roll back. Connect only through the read-write and read-only endpoints, avoid connecting to individual nodes. Add retry logic with exponential backoff for transient connection errors. Keep transactions short, because long-running transactions delay planned failover and increase the work that's rolled back during unplanned failover.
- **Account for by-design behaviors:** A reader node that becomes the writer node must handle the full write and read workload. All nodes in a pool share the same compute configuration, so choose the pool's compute size for the writer node's workload.

    The service manages the maintenance schedule. When the cluster has reader nodes, maintenance uses a planned failover. Failover is fast because the nodes share storage, so a reader node takes over without copying data or rewinding the write-ahead log. An unplanned failover also includes the time the service needs to detect the failure. In both cases, applications reconnect through the read-write endpoint. Temporary tablespaces don’t survive a restart or failover, so use them only for temporary data, such as temporary tables and sorts that spill to disk.

    Factor these behaviors into your availability targets, and confirm the service-level agreement (SLA) for your configuration in [SLAs for Online Services](https://aka.ms/csla).
- **Monitor health and get notified early:** Azure HorizonDB sends platform metrics to Azure Monitor, where you can view them under **Monitoring** > **Metrics** for the cluster and use them in alert rules. For availability, alert on *Postgres Instance Is Alive*, split by node, so you know when any node stops responding. Also watch the metrics that often change before a visible outage: *Failed Connections*, *Active Connections* compared to *Max Connections*, *Commit Latency* and *Write Latency*, *CPU percent* and *Memory percent*, *Oldest Transaction*, and *Maximum Used Transaction IDs*.

    Use Azure Resource Health to detect resource health changes, and route alerts to the people who own the workload. Also monitor the services the workload depends on: Microsoft Entra ID for sign-in, private endpoint connectivity, and Microsoft Foundry model endpoints if you use AI features.
- **Plan backup, restore, and recovery objectives:** The service takes storage snapshots several times a day and archives WAL continuously to zone-redundant storage. You can set backup retention from 1 to 35 days and restore to any point within that period. Backups longer than 35 days aren't available, so if you need to keep data longer for compliance, export it separately and save it in storage that you manage. Restore time depends on the WAL replay needed, not on database size. Restores create a new cluster, so plan how the application switches to it.

    Limit who can delete production clusters through Azure RBAC to prevent accidental deletion. Set your recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) based on these behaviors, and test restores regularly to measure how long recovery takes for your workload. For details, see [Business continuity in Azure HorizonDB](/en-us/azure/horizondb/backup-restore/concepts-business-continuity).
- **Plan for a regional outage with geo-redundant backups:** Cross-region protection is based on geo-redundant backups, which are available only in paired regions. You can choose geo-redundant backup storage only when you create the cluster, so decide whether you need it before you deploy.

    With geo-redundant backup storage, backups are copied to another region. If the cluster's primary region becomes unavailable, you restore a new cluster in the other region from those backups. Backups reach the other region with a delay, so changes made after the most recent copy aren't included in the restore. Restoring the database is only part of the recovery. The restored cluster has new endpoints, so ensure that the application can reach it through the required network connectivity and private endpoints. If the application also runs in the affected region, fail it over to an available region and update its configuration to connect to the restored cluster.

    Test a geo-restore to measure recovery time against your RTO for regional outages, and document the procedure. For details, see [Business continuity in Azure HorizonDB](/en-us/azure/horizondb/backup-restore/concepts-business-continuity).
- **Perform failure mode analysis:** Identify how each failure affects the workload and how the service or your design mitigates it.

    | Failure | Mitigation |
    | --- | --- |
    | Writer node fails | With at least one reader node, the service fails over automatically. Without a reader node, the service restarts the node and, if that fails, provisions new compute, which takes longer. |
    | Availability zone outage | Storage and backups are zone-redundant. If the cluster uses the ZoneRedundant option, a reader node in another zone becomes the writer node. |
    | Data is deleted or corrupted by mistake | Restore to a point in time before the change, into a new cluster. Manually retrieve the deleted or corrupted data. |
    | Scheduled maintenance | With reader nodes, maintenance uses a planned failover, which is fast because the nodes share storage. Connection retry logic in the application handles the switch. |
    | Region outage | If geo-redundant backups are enabled, restore a new cluster in the paired region, then redirect the application. |
    | AI model endpoint is unavailable or throttled | Azure HorizonDB AI functions and AI pipelines call Microsoft Foundry models from inside the database, so a model outage or throttling causes those SQL calls to fail. AI pipelines retry failed steps and resume from the last completed step. For AI functions that the application calls in its queries, handle errors and retry. Avoid calling a model inside a transaction that writes business data: generate embeddings and other AI output separately, for example with an asynchronous AI pipeline, so writes still succeed when the model isn't available. |
- **Scale for your load patterns:** You add or remove reader nodes online, without affecting the rest of the cluster, and storage grows automatically, so you don't need to plan storage capacity or IOPS. Match compute changes to how load arrives. For scheduled or predictable peaks, such as month-end processing or a product launch, add reader nodes or vCores ahead of the peak and remove them afterward, and automate the change with the Azure CLI or your deployment pipeline. Scaling vCores up or down doesn't noticeably interrupt applications. For unpredictable load, keep enough headroom on the writer node and the reader nodes to absorb a spike, and alert on CPU and connection thresholds so you can add capacity before users notice. Maintain at least two nodes in the default pool, because removing the last reader node disables high availability.

sections.heading: Configuration recommendations
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
| Recommendation | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
| Configure at least one reader node in the default pool (two nodes in total) for production clusters. | Provides high availability, with automatic failover if the writer node fails. With the pool's high availability option set to ZoneRedundant, it also protects against an availability zone outage. |
| Set the pool's high availability option to *ZoneRedundant* for production clusters in regions with availability zones. | Guarantees that compute spans at least two availability zones, so the cluster stays available if a zone fails. *AnyZone* doesn't guarantee cross-zone placement. |
| Connect applications through the cluster endpoints: the read-write endpoint for writes and the read-only endpoint for reads. Implement retry logic with exponential backoff. | The read-write endpoint follows the writer node after failover, the read-only endpoint spreads reads across the reader nodes, and retries let the application reconnect without manual intervention. |
| Set backup retention (1 to 35 days) to cover the longest period in which you might need to recover from data corruption or a mistaken change. | Lets you restore to a point before a problem that went unnoticed for days. |
| Enable geo-redundant backup storage when you create clusters in paired regions that must recover from a regional outage. | Keeps a copy of the backups in the paired region, so you can restore the cluster there. You can't enable it after the cluster is created. |
| Create Resource Health alerts for the cluster. | Notifies the operations team about resource health changes. |

sections.heading: Security
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
The purpose of the Security pillar is to provide **confidentiality, integrity, and availability** guarantees to the workload.

The [Security design principles](/en-us/azure/well-architected/security/principles) provide a high-level design strategy for achieving those goals by applying approaches to the technical design of Azure HorizonDB.

sections.heading: Workload design checklist
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Start your design strategy based on the [design review checklist for Security](../security/checklist) and identify vulnerabilities and controls to improve the security posture. Extend the strategy to include more approaches as needed.

- **Review the security guidance and reduce the attack surface:** Review [Security in Azure HorizonDB](/en-us/azure/horizondb/security/security-overview) to understand the security controls that the service provides and the ones you configure. Keep the cluster's exposure small. Allow only the network sources that need access. Extensions run inside the database engine with broad access to data, so keep an allow list of only the PostgreSQL extensions the workload uses, and review it when the workload changes. Remove default privileges that the workload doesn't need, such as the ability for any role to create objects in the `public` schema.
- **Use Microsoft Entra authentication only, and least privilege for access:** Use Microsoft Entra authentication only, for both people and applications, so you manage identities, multifactor authentication, and access reviews centrally and don't have database passwords to protect. Applications that run on Azure should connect with managed identities, which removes stored credentials from application configuration. If you must also enable PostgreSQL authentication, create dedicated PostgreSQL roles with least-privilege grants for each application. Use Azure role-based access control (Azure RBAC) to control who can manage the cluster. Create custom roles with actions a job needs, for example to let a team add reader nodes without being able to delete the cluster. Inside the database, grant each application and team a role with only the privileges it needs, and use row-level security when different users must see different rows of the same table. Review role memberships regularly.
- **Choose the network model before you create the cluster:** Clusters use public access with IP firewall rules, private endpoints, or both. The connectivity method can't be changed after the cluster is created, so decide it up front. Firewall rules are set for each pool and accept IPv4 addresses only. No addresses are allowed by default. Avoid the option to 'allow all Azure services' as it allows connections from other subscriptions. Always connect by fully qualified domain name, because the cluster's IP address can change. For production, use private endpoints so that traffic stays within your virtual network.
- **Encrypt data at rest:** Data, WAL, and backups are always encrypted at rest with service-managed keys. For highly sensitive data, consider client-side encryption, and use the PostgreSQL Anonymizer extension to mask data for users who shouldn't see it.
- **Encrypt data in transit:** Set the minimum protocol version to TLS 1.3 when your clients support it, and have clients verify the server certificate and host name. Trust the published root certificate authorities, not intermediate or cluster certificates, because those rotate without notice.
- **Control what data reaches AI models:** AI functions and AI pipelines send text from your tables to Microsoft Foundry model endpoints. Decide which tables and columns can be sent to a model, and keep regulated or highly sensitive data out of AI calls unless your compliance rules allow it. If you register your own models, the endpoint key is stored in the model registry, so limit who can read the registry.
- **Monitor and audit security events:** Enable auditing with the pgaudit extension for the statement classes your compliance rules require, and send the server and audit logs to a Log Analytics workspace through diagnostic settings. From there you can query them and keep them for as long as your retention policy requires. Review the Azure activity log for control-plane changes, and track the *Failed Connections* metric to spot brute-force attempts or misconfigured clients.

sections.heading: Configuration recommendations
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
| Recommendation | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
| Use private endpoints for production clusters. If you use public access, allow only specific IPv4 addresses in each pool's firewall rules, or disable public access. Don't enable access from all Azure services. | Keeps database traffic on private networks and limits who can reach the cluster. |
| Set `ssl_min_protocol_version` to `TLSv1.3`, and keep `require_secure_transport` set to `ON`. | Rejects connections that use older or no encryption. |
| Configure clients to verify the server certificate and host name, and trust the current Azure root CAs. | Protects against man-in-the-middle attacks and keeps connections working through certificate rotations. |
| Use Microsoft Entra authentication only, and connect applications with managed identities. | Centralizes identity management and removes database passwords from application configuration. |
| If you must enable PostgreSQL authentication, set `password_encryption` to `SCRAM-SHA-256` and allow only the SCRAM-SHA-256 method. Create dedicated PostgreSQL roles with least-privilege grants for each application, and don't use the administrator login in applications. | Protects passwords in transit and at rest with salted hashing, and limits what a compromised password can access. |
| Revoke `CREATE` permissions on the `public` schema from `PUBLIC`, and grant each role only the privileges it needs. | Limits the damage a compromised identity can do. |
| Set `azure.extensions` to only the extensions the workload needs. | Reduces the attack surface by blocking extensions you don't use. |
| Grant AI model access per user with the model registry functions, and give `model_registry_manager` only to the people who manage models. | Limits who can send data to AI models and who can change model endpoints. |
| Enable pgaudit, set `pgaudit.log` to the statement classes required by your compliance rules, and send audit logs to Log Analytics. | Records database activity for investigations and audits, and keeps the logs outside the database. |
| Assign Azure RBAC roles for cluster management by least privilege. Use custom roles with only the `Microsoft.HorizonDB` actions each team needs, and limit who can delete clusters. | Prevents unauthorized configuration changes and deletion. |

sections.heading: Cost Optimization
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Cost Optimization focuses on **detecting spend patterns, prioritizing investments in critical areas, and optimizing in others** to meet the organization's budget while meeting business requirements.

The [Cost Optimization design principles](/en-us/azure/well-architected/cost-optimization/principles) provide a high-level design strategy for achieving those goals and making tradeoffs as necessary in the technical design related to Azure HorizonDB and its environment.

sections.heading: Workload design checklist
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Start your design strategy based on the [design review checklist for Cost Optimization](../cost-optimization/checklist) for investments. Fine-tune the design to align the workload with the allocated budget. Your design should use the right Azure capabilities, monitor investments, and find opportunities to optimize over time.

- **Create and maintain a cost model:** Estimate the cost of each environment with the [Azure pricing calculator](https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/calculator/). Include the main cost drivers: compute for every node, billed per vCore-hour; storage, billed per GiB used, which grows with the data; and backup storage beyond a free amount equal to the database size. Write-heavy workloads, longer backup retention, and geo-redundant backup storage all increase backup storage. Also include the costs around the cluster: Log Analytics ingestion and retention for diagnostic and audit logs, private endpoint charges, and Microsoft Foundry model usage if you use AI features. After the workload is in production, compare the model with actual spending in Microsoft Cost Management and update it.
- **Keep secondary costs under control:** Set backup retention to the period you actually need, and use geo-redundant backup storage only for clusters that must recover from a regional outage. Send only the log categories you use to Log Analytics, and set workspace retention to match your policy. Use one private endpoint per cluster and share it across application networks through virtual network peering. Run the application in the same region as the cluster to avoid data transfer charges.
- **Use the database savings plan for steady compute:** For production compute that runs continuously at a predictable size, use the database savings plan, which lowers the compute price in exchange for a one-year or three-year commitment. Keep pay-as-you-go for environments that you resize or delete often.
- **Optimize AI model calls to control cost:** The number of AI calls drives AI cost, especially embedding generation for large tables. Store embeddings instead of generating them again, set an incremental column on AI pipeline sources so later runs process only new or changed rows, and run a full backfill only when you change the model or the embedding dimensions. Pause pipelines with `on_change` triggers while you tune them.
- **Make costs visible and set guardrails:** Tag clusters by workload, environment, and owner, and set budgets and alerts in Microsoft Cost Management. Because storage grows automatically, set alerts on the *Storage Used* and *Backup Storage Used* metrics so unexpected growth doesn't go unnoticed. Limit who can scale vCores or add reader nodes through Azure RBAC.
- **Configure each environment for its purpose:** Development and test clusters usually don't need reader nodes or large vCore sizes. Keep high availability and reader nodes for production and for environments that test failover or performance. Stop development and test pools when they aren't in use, for example outside working hours. Stopping a pool deallocates its compute, so you don't pay for compute while it's stopped. Use the shortest backup retention and local backup storage in nonproduction, unless you test recovery procedures there.
- **Adjust capacity to demand:** Review CPU and memory use regularly and scale vCores down when the workload doesn't need them. Scaling down doesn't noticeably interrupt applications, so you can adjust the size as needed. Add reader nodes for peak read demand and remove them when demand drops. The read-only endpoint balances connections across the current set of reader nodes, so the application doesn't need to change. Reader nodes are quick to add because they don't copy data. Keep at least one reader node in production, because removing the last one disables high availability.
- **Consolidate where isolation requirements allow:** A cluster can host several databases, which share its compute and storage. Consolidation lowers cost, but the databases also share firewall rules, server parameters, the maintenance window, and failover events, and a busy database can slow down the others. Consolidate databases with similar security, availability, and performance requirements.

    Use per-database metrics, such as transactions and database size, to watch each database's resource use. Keep databases with different compliance or availability requirements in separate clusters. For multitenant workloads, match the cluster model to each tenant's cost profile: place tenants with standard requirements together, either a database per tenant or a shared schema with a tenant ID column and row-level security, and give tenants that pay for higher isolation or availability their own cluster. Use per-database metrics and resource tags to attribute cost to each tenant.

sections.heading: Configuration recommendations
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
| Recommendation | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
| Size vCores based on observed *CPU percent* and *Memory percent* metrics, and review the size regularly. | Avoids paying for unused compute on every node. |
| Use the database savings plan for production compute with stable usage. | Lowers compute cost compared to pay-as-you-go. |
| Set backup retention and backup storage redundancy per environment. | Avoids paying for long retention and geo-redundant backups where you don't need them. |
| Set the number of reader nodes based on your availability and read-scale requirements together, not separately. | Each reader node is billed for its vCores, and the same reader nodes provide both failover and read capacity. |
| Route read-only traffic to the read-only endpoint before you increase vCores. | Uses read capacity you already pay for on the reader nodes instead of buying more compute. |
| Disable high availability on development and test clusters. | Removes the cost of reader nodes where you don't need them. |
| Stop development and test pools when they aren't in use. | Deallocates compute, so you don't pay for it while the pool is stopped. |
| Set alerts on *Storage Used* and *Backup Storage Used*. | Catches storage growth, which has no upper limit by default, before it affects the budget. |
| Tag clusters and set budgets in Microsoft Cost Management. | Shows cost per workload and environment and warns before you exceed the budget. |
| Keep the query store retention (`pg_qs.retention_period_in_days`) no longer than you need. | Avoids storing performance data you won't use. |
| Set an incremental column on AI pipeline sources, and run full backfills only when the model or embedding dimensions change. | Avoids paying to generate embeddings again for rows that didn't change. |

sections.heading: Operational Excellence
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Operational Excellence primarily focuses on procedures for **development practices, observability, and release management**.

The [Operational Excellence design principles](/en-us/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/principles) provide a high-level design strategy for achieving those goals for the operational requirements of the workload.

sections.heading: Workload design checklist
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Start your design strategy based on the [design review checklist for Operational Excellence](../operational-excellence/checklist) for defining processes for observability, testing, and deployment related to Azure HorizonDB.

- **Deploy with infrastructure as code:** Define clusters, pools, nodes, network rules, and parameter groups in Bicep or Terraform, or script them with the Azure CLI. Some settings, such as the connectivity method, can't be changed after the cluster is created, so get them right in the template. Manage database schema changes with a migration tool in the same pipeline, and test them on a nonproduction cluster first. Plan how to roll back before you deploy: make schema changes backward compatible where you can, so the previous application version still works, and keep a tested rollback script for each change. For changes that modify data, note the time before you deploy, so you can restore to that point in a new cluster if you need to.
- **Keep configuration consistent and automate routine work:** Manage server parameters through parameter groups and attach the same group to the pools that should match, so configuration doesn't drift between environments. The service handles patching and minor version upgrades during system-managed maintenance windows. It also manages backups and storage growth. Use pg\_cron for scheduled database jobs. PostgreSQL autovacuum reclaims space from obsolete row versions and updates query-planner statistics. Consider adaptive autovacuum to adjust its settings automatically as the workload changes.
- **Build monitoring around the metrics that matter:** Azure HorizonDB sends platform metrics to Azure Monitor, including CPU and memory use, connections, transactions per second, commit and write latency, cache hit ratios, logical replication lag, oldest transaction age, bloat, and vacuum activity. Compute metrics are emitted for each node, so you can see the load on the writer node and on every reader node separately, and many metrics can also be split by database.

    Build dashboards and alerts on these metrics. Send server logs to a Log Analytics workspace through diagnostic settings so you can query them alongside application logs, and use the query store and Query Performance Insight to find slow and frequent queries. If you use AI pipelines, check `ai.status()` regularly, and verify the output by counting the rows that have results, such as embeddings, not only the rows processed.
- **Prepare for incidents and validate changes:** Subscribe to Resource Health alerts so you learn about resource health changes quickly, and use Resource Health to check whether a problem is on the platform side. Use planned failover to test that applications reconnect correctly. Restore backups to a new cluster on a schedule to confirm that your recovery procedure works. Don't change the cluster's configuration while maintenance is in progress. Failover mechanics are described in the Reliability section.

sections.heading: Configuration recommendations
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
| Recommendation | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
| Deploy clusters, pools, nodes, network rules, and parameter groups from Bicep or Terraform in a pipeline. | Makes deployments repeatable and reviewable, and keeps environments consistent. |
| Attach a shared parameter group to the pools that should have the same configuration. | Prevents configuration drift between clusters and environments. |
| Configure diagnostic settings to send server logs to a Log Analytics workspace. | Keeps logs available for troubleshooting and correlation with application logs. |
| Create metric alerts for *CPU percent*, *Memory percent*, *Active Connections* compared to *Max Connections*, *Storage Used*, *Oldest Transaction*, and *Postgres Instance Is Alive*, split by node. | Detects resource pressure, connection exhaustion, long-running transactions, and outages before users report them. |
| Set `pg_qs.query_capture_mode` to `top` for production clusters. | Captures the queries clients run without the extra overhead of tracking nested statements. |
| Run planned failovers on a schedule. | Confirms that applications reconnect correctly and that runbooks are up to date. |

sections.heading: Performance Efficiency
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Performance Efficiency is about **maintaining user experience even when there's an increase in load** by managing capacity. The strategy includes scaling resources, identifying and optimizing potential bottlenecks, and optimizing for peak performance.

The [Performance Efficiency design principles](/en-us/azure/well-architected/performance-efficiency/principles) provide a high-level design strategy for achieving those capacity goals against the expected usage.

sections.heading: Workload design checklist
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Start your design strategy based on the [design review checklist for Performance Efficiency](../performance-efficiency/checklist). Define a baseline that's based on key performance indicators for Azure HorizonDB.

- **Plan capacity from a measured baseline:** Compute sizes range from 2 to 192 vCores, with 8 GB of memory per vCore. Storage scales automatically and doesn't need IOPS provisioning. Load test with production-like data and queries, and record CPU, memory, transactions per second, commit latency, and cache hit ratios as your baseline. Choose the vCore size that meets your latency and throughput targets with headroom for peaks. You can scale up vCores without a noticeable interruption, so you can start smaller and scale up as the workload grows.

    Azure HorizonDB offers AMD and Intel processors. Choose between them based on the same load test: run it on both, and compare throughput and latency against the price per vCore-hour, because price-performance depends on the workload's mix of queries. Check that the processor you choose is available in your regions, and use the same processor in test and production, so that performance results from testing apply to production.
- **Scale reads out and writes up:** Every reader node is readable, so plan to offload read-heavy work, such as reporting, dashboards, search, and API reads, to the reader nodes, and keep the writer node for writes. Writes go only to the writer node, so write throughput depends on the vCore size. Reads can scale out across up to 15 reader nodes, and the read-only endpoint balances connections across them automatically. Reader nodes can lag the writer node by milliseconds, so send reads that need the latest committed data to the read-write endpoint. When a cluster has no reader nodes, the read-only endpoint routes to the writer node and doesn't reject writes. Don't rely on this endpoint to enforce read-only access. Grant read-only database privileges to roles that must not write.
- **Monitor performance and validate against the baseline:** Track latency, throughput, wait events, and cache hit ratios in Azure Monitor, and alert on deviations from the baseline. Use the query store, wait sampling, and Query Performance Insight to find the queries and waits that use the most resources. Repeat load tests after schema changes, major application releases, and vCore changes.
- **Design vector and AI workloads for performance:** Use DiskANN as the vector index for production workloads. It evaluates filters inside the index walk, so recall and latency stay steady when queries filter by tenant, category, or date, and it supports up to 16,000 dimensions. Add B-tree indexes on the columns that vector queries filter on, such as a tenant ID or category, so the planner can combine the filter with the vector index. For more than a million vectors, enable spherical quantization to reduce memory use. Tune `diskann.l_value_is` to balance recall against latency. Run vector and hybrid search queries on the reader nodes through the read-only endpoint. AI pipelines run on the writer node, so schedule large backfills outside peak hours.
- **Tune the cache, connections, and queries:** Each node has a local NVMe SSD cache for frequently used pages. Watch the *SSD Cache Hit Ratio* and *Buffer Pool Cache Hit Ratio* metrics. Caches are per node, so a new writer node after failover, or a reader node after scaling, starts with a cold cache. Use an external connection pooler, especially for applications that open many short-lived connections. Set statement and idle-in-transaction timeouts to stop runaway sessions. Keep autovacuum effective to limit bloat. Deploy the application in the same region as the cluster to keep network latency low.

sections.heading: Configuration recommendations
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
| Recommendation | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
| Choose the processor type (AMD or Intel) for each pool from a load test on both, and use the same type in test and production. | Gets the best price-performance for the workload, and keeps test results valid for production. |
| Send read-only queries that tolerate a delay of milliseconds to the read-only endpoint. | Spreads read load across reader nodes and frees the writer node for writes. |
| Connect applications through an external connection pooler | Reduces connection overhead and keeps connections below `max_connections`. |
| Enable query store and wait sampling, and review the top queries regularly. | Shows which queries and waits to optimize first. |
| Set `statement_timeout` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` for application roles. | Stops long-running and idle sessions that hold resources and block vacuum. |
| Enable adaptive autovacuum (`adaptive_autovacuum.optimize_configurations`). | Adjusts autovacuum to the workload and limits table bloat. |
| Set `azure.enable_temp_tablespaces_on_local_ssd` to `ON` for workloads with heavy sorts or temporary tables. | Places temporary objects on fast local storage. |
| Deploy application compute in the same region as the cluster. | Reduces network latency for every query. |
| Use Fabric mirroring (`azure.fabric_mirror_enabled`) for analytical and reporting queries over large data sets. | Moves analytical load to Microsoft Fabric so it doesn't compete with transactional queries on the cluster. |

sections.heading: Tradeoffs
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
You might need to make design trade-offs when you use the approaches in the pillar checklists. The following sections highlight the advantages and drawbacks of key decisions.

**Add reader nodes**

Adding reader nodes enables automatic failover and increases the cluster's read capacity. The trade-off is higher cost because each reader node is billed for its full vCore allocation.

**Choose ZoneRedundant instead of AnyZone**

Choosing *ZoneRedundant* ensures that compute spans at least two zones, providing higher availability. This choice can increase provisioning time because the service must obtain capacity in at least two availability zones before provisioning can complete.

**Enable geo-redundant backup storage**

Enabling geo-redundant backup storage (where available) allows you to restore the cluster in the paired Azure region after a region outage, at the cost of higher backup storage charges.

**Use the database savings plan**

The database savings plan lowers compute costs but requires a fixed hourly spending commitment for one or three years. If usage falls below that commitment, you still pay the committed amount, which might reduce your flexibility to downsize.

**Read from reader nodes**

Reading from reader nodes spreads the read load and frees the writer node for write operations. Because reader nodes can lag behind the writer node, applications must tolerate slightly stale reads.

**Require TLS 1.3**

Requiring TLS 1.3 ensures that the strongest protocol version is used for secure communication, but prevents older drivers and tools that support only TLS 1.2 from connecting.

**Use private endpoints instead of public access**

Using private endpoints keeps database traffic on private networks while requiring private DNS configuration and network connectivity for every client, including administrators.

**Consolidate databases on one cluster**

Consolidating databases on one cluster shares compute, replicas, and storage, reducing costs. In exchange, databases share network rules, parameters, maintenance, and failover, and compete for resources.

**Capture all queries in query store**

Capturing all queries in the query store provides complete visibility into nested statements, which helps with performance tuning and troubleshooting. However, it adds processing overhead that can affect database performance and increases storage consumption and costs.

**Run AI calls inside the database**

Running AI calls inside the database keeps data local and ensures embeddings are up to date. However, it incurs model usage costs and sends table data to model endpoints. Assess the data sensitivity, endpoint access controls, and compliance requirements before enabling these calls.

sections.heading: Azure policies
headings: Architecture best practices for Azure HorizonDB
sections.text:
Azure provides built-in policy definitions that you can use to audit and enforce configuration across your Azure HorizonDB clusters. Use the following built-in policy so that every cluster sends its logs to Log Analytics, without relying on each team to configure diagnostic settings:

- Deploy Diagnostic Settings for Azure HorizonDB clusters to Log Analytics workspace

For more information, see [Azure Policy built-in policy definitions](/en-us/azure/governance/policy/samples/built-in-policies).

For more information, see [Azure Advisor](/en-us/azure/advisor/advisor-overview).
